Arithmetic

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 20k Articles: 356
Arithmetic studies operations on numbers: combining quantities by addition, finding differences by subtraction, scaling through multiplication, and reversing a nonzero scale through division. Its usefulness goes beyond producing an answer. A calculation can express how resources are shared, how a measurement changes with scale, or why two different descriptions of a quantity agree.
The allowed numbers matter. Start with the natural numbers 0,1,2,…. Counting collections gives 2+3=5, but removing three from two calls for the integer −1. Sharing three units equally between two recipients gives the rational number 3/2. These operations motivate larger number systems: integers supply additive inverses, and rational numbers supply division by nonzero integers. A real number can also express lengths such as a diagonal of Euclidean norm 2​, which is not a rational number.
The beauty is that bookkeeping, geometry, and algebra can check one another. The same product 3(2+4)=18 counts three groups of six, measures the area of a rectangle, and splits as 3⋅2+3⋅4 by distributivity. A number line makes negative integers visible as positions; a fraction records an exact share even when its decimal representation does not terminate. An arithmetic rule becomes easier to remember when these interpretations fit together.

Number

Arithmetic OurBigBook.com
Numbers are mathematical objects used to express quantities and carry out operations. Familiar families include the natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, real numbers, and complex numbers; specifying the family determines which operations and solutions are available.

Surreal number

Number OurBigBook.com

Division (mathematics, a/b)

Words: 718 Articles: 8
Arithmetic OurBigBook.com
For real numbers a and b=0, division a/b asks for the unique number x satisfying bx=a. Equivalently, a/b=ab−1 uses the multiplicative inverse of b. This description separates the role of the denominator from the result: the quotient undoes a specified multiplication.
For example, 3/2 is the number whose double is three, so it is exactly 1.5. A second interpretation asks how many portions of size 2 fit into an amount 3; the answer is one and a half portions. Equal sharing and measuring with a specified portion size lead to the same quotient, although the units assigned to the result can differ.
In the natural numbers, exact division need not be possible. Euclidean division instead keeps a remainder: 17=5⋅3+2, with 0≤2<5. Thus seventeen objects form three complete groups of five with two left over. As a rational number, the same quotient is 17/5=3+2/5=3.4. The remainder and the fractional part describe the same unfinished group in different ways.
Division by zero cannot retain the unique-solution rule. For a=0, the equation 0x=a has no solution; for a=0, every real number x solves 0x=0, so there is no unique quotient. This explains both failures through multiplication, rather than assigning a/0 a value that would contradict ordinary arithmetic. [ref]

Integer division

Words: 355 Articles: 3
Division (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
Division of integers that returns an integer quotient rather than an exact fraction. A rounding convention is required for negative operands. For n≥0 and d>0, the quotient is q=⌊n/d⌋ and the remainder is r=n−qd with 0≤r<d.

Packed restoring division (pk​=bQk​+Rk​)

Words: 141
Integer division OurBigBook.com
For an n-bit unsigned dividend a and positive divisor b, read the dividend bits from most to least significant. If the processed prefix is p, maintain p=bQ+R with 0≤R<b. Appending bit d gives trial remainder T=2R+d; append quotient bit [T≥b] and replace the remainder by T−b[T≥b]. This preserves the quotient–remainder identity.
The old dividend and new quotient can share one n-bit processor register: after k iterations its value is (a2kmod2n)+Qk​, where Qk​<2k. The shifted dividend occupies the upper positions and the accumulated quotient occupies the lower positions, so no information is overwritten. The high processor register holds Rk​. For an n-bit dividend the next trial remainder is no larger than the next prefix, hence fits in n bits through the final iteration. This last bound is specific to the dividend width; it must not be assumed for unrestricted multiword dividends.

Signed power-of-two division by biasing (trunc(a/2k)=⌊(a+(2k−1)1a<0​)/2k⌋)

Words: 105
Integer division OurBigBook.com
For signed two's complement integers, a conditional positive bias converts the rounding behaviour of an arithmetic right shift into C integer division. It can be formed without a conditional branch by turning the sign bit into either zero or a low-k-bit bit mask.
Proof. Nonnegative a needs no adjustment. If a<0, write −a=2kq+r, 0≤r<2k. Then a+(2k−1)=−2kq+(2k−1−r), whose quotient rounded down is −q, exactly the quotient truncated towards zero. The bias fits safely for 1≤k<n in an n-bit signed word: it is added only to negative inputs, and the largest possible adjusted input is 2k−2. The corresponding remainder is ((a+b)mod2k)−b, where b=(2k−1)1a<0​.

C integer division (a=bq+r,q=trunc(a/b))

Words: 73
Integer division OurBigBook.com
For representable integer quotients with nonzero divisor, C integer division discards the fractional part towards zero and defines the remainder by a=bq+r. Thus a nonzero remainder has the dividend's sign. For example, −13=5(−2)+(−3), so division by five returns quotient −2 and remainder −3. This convention differs from division rounded down, which would return quotient −3 and nonnegative remainder 2. Division by zero and an unrepresentable quotient are excluded.[ref]

Ratio (a:b)

Words: 161 Articles: 2
Division (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
A ratio compares two quantities a,b, written a:b and corresponding to division a/b when b=0. Equal ratios of corresponding lengths characterize the scaling of similar triangles.
For example, 6:4 and 3:2 specify the same ratio because 6/4=3/2. Multiplying both entries by the same nonzero scale preserves the quotient: (ca)/(cb)=a/b. This is useful when comparing mixtures or scaling a recipe; doubling both ingredient amounts preserves their ratio, while adding the same amount to both generally does not. For quantities with the same physical units, their ratio is dimensionless, connecting this elementary calculation with dimensional analysis.

Percentage (x%=x/100)

Words: 70 Articles: 1
Ratio OurBigBook.com
A percentage expresses a ratio in hundredths: p as a fraction is 100p%. For example, 18/60=0.3=30%. Comparing two percentages requires specifying whether the change is an absolute difference in percentage points or a relative change divided by the initial value.
Percentage point (pp)
Words: 33
Percentage OurBigBook.com
A percentage point is one hundredth on a probability or proportion scale. A change from 20% to 25% is 5 percentage points, while the relative increase is (25−20)/20=25%. These answer different questions and have different denominators.

Inequality (mathematics, a<b,a≤b)

Words: 209 Articles: 3
Arithmetic OurBigBook.com
An inequality compares mathematical quantities using an ordering, such as a<b or a≤b for real numbers. A strict inequality excludes equality; a non-strict inequality allows it. For example, 4<5 is strict, while 4≤4 is true because equality is allowed. Adding the same real number preserves either comparison; multiplying by a negative real number reverses its direction.

Strict inequality (a<b)

Words: 30
Inequality (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
An ordered comparison such as a<b, excluding equality. In a sorted search, strict comparisons distinguish regions that can be discarded from boundary positions that may contain an equal target.

Linear inequality (aTx≤b)

Words: 130 Articles: 1
Inequality (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
A linear inequality compares a linear functional of a vector of unknowns with a constant, for example aTx≤b or aTx<b over the real numbers. For a=0, its solution set is a closed or open half-space, respectively. The inequality x+y≤1 allows all points on one side of the line x+y=1, including the line. Multiplication by a negative real number reverses the inequality, so x≥1 is equivalently −x≤−1.

System of linear inequalities (Ax≤b)

Words: 68
Linear inequality OurBigBook.com
A system of linear inequalities requires several linear inequalities to hold simultaneously. The notation Ax≤b compares coordinates componentwise, giving one inequality per row of the matrix A. Its solution set is the intersection of the corresponding half-spaces. For non-strict inequalities it is a linear polyhedron, which may be empty. For example, x≥1, y≥1, x+y≤1 are inconsistent: adding their equivalent forms −x≤−1, −y≤−1, x+y≤1 gives 0≤−1. A Farkas certificate for linear inequalities generalizes this cancellation.

Sum of squares (∑i​ai2​)

Words: 41
Arithmetic OurBigBook.com
A sum of squares adds the squares of numbers ai2​ for specified real numbers ai​. It is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when every term is zero. For the coordinates of a vector, it is the squared Euclidean norm; for regression residuals, it gives the residual sum of squares minimized by ordinary least squares.

Pair the rows with a reversed copy: 1+n=2+(n−1)=⋯=n+1. There are n such pairs, so two copies contain n(n+1) dots. Dividing by two proves the formula. This rectangle picture explains the factor one-half without requiring a formula for a long summation. For example, one hundred rows contain T100​=5050 dots.
The same count appears whenever every pair of different objects must be considered once. Five participants make ten possible handshakes; five sensors have ten different pairwise comparisons; a complete graph on five vertices has ten edges. These are the triangular number pair-counting identity, with one fewer row than objects. The distinction prevents a common error: T5​=15 counts all pairs from six objects, whereas five objects give T4​=10.
The triangular number square-complement identity says that two neighboring triangular numbers fill a square. Combining that identity with the one-row difference makes the difference of squares Tn2​−Tn−12​ equal to n3. It leads to Nicomachus's theorem: the sum of the first n cubes of numbers is the square of a number Tn2​. A change in the way one groups objects exposes a relation between summation, multiplication and geometry.
This geometric view is already visible in Nicomachus's Introduction to Arithmetic by Nicomachus (Hahn teacher edition): Book II, Chapter 8 describes growing triangular rows, Chapter 12 combines successive triangular counts into squares, and Chapter 20 groups successive odd integers into cubes of numbers.[ref] The linked edition uses Martin Luther D'Ooge's translation, revised with modern teaching material by Nathanael Hahn. Our empty-row index T0​=0 is a modern convention; the historical passage starts from unity and calls three the first actual triangle.

Its usefulness becomes immediate for successive growth factors. Suppose a hypothetical positive quantity starts at Q0​=1000, is multiplied by 3/2, then by 2/3. For a real sequence (an​), the partial sum of ∑k=1∞​(ak​−ak−1​) is exactly an​−a0​. Consequently it is a convergent series if and only if an​ has a finite limit L, and its sum is L−a0​. Cancellation takes place inside each finite partial sum; taking a limit is a separate step.[ref]
The partial fraction telescoping example has SN​=N/(3N+1) and therefore limit 1/3. In contrast, let an​=(−1)n. Its first entry is a0​=1, so SN​=(−1)N−1. The even partial sums are zero and the odd partial sums are negative two. Both finite cancellations are correct, but the sequence has no single limit, giving a divergent series.
It is also essential to keep the two contributions paired. For example, ∑k=1∞​(1/k−1/(k+1)) is a convergent series with sum one, as its finite partial sum is 1−1/(N+1). Writing it instead as ∑k=1∞​1/k−∑k=1∞​1/(k+1) asks to subtract two divergent series. The permitted finite cancellation does not define that separate subtraction. Working through partial sums keeps the indices aligned and the operation meaningful.

Sum OurBigBook.com
An empty sum has no terms and is defined to be zero, the identity element for addition. This keeps the rule for combining sums valid when one index set is empty. In a Galton-Watson process, an empty generation contributes an empty sum of offspring counts, so the next generation is empty too. The corresponding convention for multiplication is the empty product, which equals one.
Weighted arithmetic mean (xˉw​)
Words: 1k Articles: 7
Sum OurBigBook.com
The weighted arithmetic mean combines values according to how much each contributes to the quantity being summarized. For a finite list of real numbers xi​ and nonnegative weights wi​ with W=∑i​wi​>0, define
xˉw​=W∑i​wi​xi​​.​
(19)
Zero weights ignore an entry; at least one weight must be positive. Multiplying every weight by the same positive number leaves the result unchanged. Writing pi​=wi​/W makes the weighted mean a convex combination, since pi​≥0 and ∑i​pi​=1. It therefore lies between the smallest and largest input values. [ref]
For example, give the values 90 and 60 weights 2 and 8:
xˉw​=2+82⋅90+8⋅60​=66​.
(20)
The larger weight pulls the result closer to 60. The balancing identity
∑i​wi​(xi​−xˉw​)=0
(21)
explains a geometric interpretation: if the weights were masses placed at positions xi​, the weighted mean would be their center of mass. Here 8(66−60)=2(90−66)=48, so the two sides balance even though their distances from the mean differ.
Weights need an interpretation. They can represent numbers of observations, masses, or probabilities in a finite probability distribution. These meanings lead to the same formula, while answering different questions. For instance, combining means of groups uses group sizes as weights to recover the mean over individual observations. For a function f and nonnegative weight function w, the analogous integral is ∫wf/∫w, provided wf is integrable and the total weight ∫w is positive and finite.

For positive mean density, this average weights a velocity by local mass rather than volume. It satisfies the exact identity ⟨ρu⟩=⟨ρ⟩u, so it naturally represents mass flux in averaged conservation laws. The ordinary volume mean generally fails that identity when density and velocity are correlated. Applied inside a phase, the same construction uses density times that phase's indicator as its weight.

For a partition of a set of complete sample observations into groups of known sizes ng​ and total N, its sample mean is the weighted mean of the group sample means. Indeed, dividing ∑g​∑i∈g​yi​=∑g​ng​y​g​ by N proves the identity. If the printed group means mg​ each have absolute rounding error at most δg​, their compatible pooled mean lies in
[∑g​Nng​​(mg​−δg​), ∑g​Nng​​(mg​+δg​)].
(22)
This follows because all the weights are nonnegative. Equivalently, the pooled absolute rounding error is at most ∑g​(ng​/N)δg​, by the triangle inequality. A printed overall mean must have a rounding interval intersecting this interval. Disjoint intervals prove incompatibility, rather than merely a difference of displayed decimals. This is a necessary consistency check for means of the same complete sample; it cannot silently equate a full-sample mean with a different complete-case mean or establish a unique repair to inconsistent output.

Each group contributes the sum nj​xˉj​; add those totals before dividing by the overall count. This is exactly a weighted mean of group means with weights equal to group sizes. [ref]
Take a synthetic example with two observations equal to 90 and eight equal to 60. The two group means are 90 and 60, and the combined mean is 66. Giving the two groups equal weights instead produces (90+60)/2=75, which summarizes the two group means with equal influence. To summarize all ten individuals with equal influence, use their group counts.
The group means and counts determine the combined arithmetic mean, but do not generally determine the combined variance. Variation within the groups is additional information.

Arithmetic mean OurBigBook.com
The harmonic mean of a nonempty finite list of positive real numbers is the multiplicative inverse of the arithmetic mean of their inverses:
H=∑i=1n​1/xi​n​,Hn​=∑i=1n​xi​1​.
(28)
For two inputs, H=2x1​x2​/(x1​+x2​). Replacing each input by H preserves the sum of inverses, making it useful when a fixed amount divided by a rate determines a cost or duration. This positive-input definition avoids division by zero; negative inputs need not retain the usual averaging or ordering properties. [ref].
Travel two legs of equal length d at positive speeds v1​,v2​, with no stops. Their travel times are d/v1​ and d/v2​, so the average speed is
vavg​=d/v1​+d/v2​2d​=1/v1​+1/v2​2​.
(29)
For two 60km legs at 30 and 60km/h, the times are two hours and one hour. The average speed is 120/3=40km/h. The same speeds maintained for one hour each instead cover 90km in two hours, giving the arithmetic mean 45km/h. A slower equal-distance leg occupies more time, so the data being averaged must include what is held equal. This is total distance traveled divided by elapsed time; a return journey can have zero average velocity while keeping a positive average speed. [ref].
The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality applied to the inverses gives H≤G; together with G≤A it yields the comparison in geometric mean. For two inputs the arithmetic–harmonic gap has the exact form
A−H=2(x1​+x2​)(x1​−x2​)2​≥0.
(30)
For 30 and 60 the gap is five. With one positive input held fixed and another approaching zero, the harmonic mean approaches zero too: a very slow fixed-distance leg dominates the travel time. Unequal leg lengths instead require a weighted harmonic mean.

wi​=∑j​dj​di​​,vavg​=∑i​di​/vi​∑i​di​​=(∑i​vi​wi​​)−1.

The two weight systems describe the same journey in different coordinates and must not be interchanged. [ref].
Prefix sum (Pm​=∑i=1m​ai​)
Words: 472 Articles: 2
Sum OurBigBook.com
A prefix sum stores the accumulated sum through a specified position in a finite sequence or array. For inputs a1​,…,an​, include the empty sum P0​=0 and set
Pm​=∑i=1m​ai​,Pm​=Pm−1​+am​(1≤m≤n).
(33)
For the original input (4,−2,5,−1,3,−4), the prefix array including P0​ is (0,4,2,7,6,9,5). A negative entry makes the accumulated sum decrease; a prefix sum does not have to be monotone. Conversely, the original entry is recovered by subtraction: am​=Pm​−Pm−1​.
The useful cancellation is that any contiguous block has sum
i=ℓ∑r​ai​=Pr​−Pℓ−1​(1≤ℓ≤r≤n).​
(34)
Both prefixes include the entries before ℓ; subtracting cancels those entries. In the example, the sum from positions two through four is −2+5−1=2, recovered as P4​−P1​=6−4. The arithmetic mean of that block is 2/3, obtained by dividing its sum by its length. Prefix sums therefore make many repeated questions about an unchanged array cheap: reuse accumulated totals instead of resumming every block.
The sequential recurrence builds all n+1 prefixes in O(n) time complexity and storage; each block query needs two reads and one subtraction, hence O(1) time complexity. These counts assume constant-cost arithmetic and access to array entries. If one input changes, all later stored prefixes change, so this simple representation is most useful when queries outnumber updates. For integer inputs, sufficient numeric capacity must be retained; with floating-point arithmetic, subtracting large nearby prefixes can lose relative accuracy for a small block total. The exact mathematical identity does not eliminate representation error.
The apparently sequential recurrence also motivates a prefix scan: associativity permits a tree of partial calculations that yields all accumulated results in parallel. Guy E. Blelloch's 1990 technical report systematically develops this operation and its applications; its authored chapter version explains the two tree sweeps used to obtain all prefixes. [ref]. [ref].

Prefix scan (sm​=a1​⊕⋯⊕am​)
Words: 122
Prefix sum OurBigBook.com
A prefix scan computes successive accumulated results for an associative operation ⊕ while keeping input order fixed. A scan based on addition produces prefix sums; one based on matrix multiplication produces successive ordered matrix products. Associativity allows regrouping, while commutativity is unnecessary because the order stays fixed. If an initial empty prefix is included, its value is the identity element for the chosen operation.
The ability to compute accumulated results does not by itself allow subtraction of two prefixes. For example, two accumulated minima cannot reveal a block minimum: the lists (1,7,8) and (1,2,3) both have successive minima (1,1,1), but the minimum of positions two through three is seven for one and two for the other. Prefix sums support block recovery because addition has additive inverses; an arbitrary associative operation need not have that property.

Subtraction (−)

Arithmetic OurBigBook.com
Subtraction adds the additive inverse: a−b=a+(−b). On the number line, 2−3=−1 is a shift three units left from 2. Reversing the two inputs changes the sign: 3−2=1, so subtraction is generally not commutative. Solving x+3=2 gives the same answer x=−1 by adding −3 to both sides; the operation preserves equality while undoing the added amount.

Borrow (bi​)

Words: 71
Subtraction OurBigBook.com
In positional subtraction, a higher place supplies one unit of its place value when the current place cannot subtract the requested digit. In binary representation, subtraction of one, a low bit toggles at every operation and the borrow continues through each zero bit, stopping at the first one bit. Thus decrementing a binary counter toggles position i exactly when all less significant bits were zero. This is the downward-counting counterpart of a carry propagating through one bits during incrementing.

Multiplication (×)

Words: 674 Articles: 19
Arithmetic OurBigBook.com
Multiplication combines two factors into their product of numbers. For a natural number n, nx is the sum of n copies of x; with no copies the result is zero. This repeated-addition interpretation directly explains integer grouping, while multiplication of arbitrary real numbers also describes scaling by noninteger factors.
A rectangle of side lengths 3 and 6 has area 18. Split the second side into lengths 2 and 4. The two areas are 6 and 12, giving the visible identity
3(2+4)=3⋅2+3⋅4=18.
(35)
Rotating the same rectangle interchanges the sides without changing its area, explaining 3⋅6=6⋅3. These pictures illustrate distributivity and commutativity for ordinary positive numbers; matrix multiplication and other operations require their own rules.
For a fractional example, take 3/2 of a quantity and then 2/3 of that result: the combined scale is (2/3)(3/2)=1. The two fractions are multiplicative inverses. In the unit square on the right, the overlap of a strip occupying 3/4 of the width with one occupying 2/3 of the height contains six of twelve equal cells. Its area is (3/4)(2/3)=1/2. The product stays exact even though the decimal expansion of 2/3 repeats. [ref]

Arithmetic progression (ak​=a1​+(k−1)d)

Words: 943 Articles: 7
Arithmetic OurBigBook.com
An arithmetic progression is a sequence with a constant common difference between consecutive sequence terms. It has the form a,a+r,…,a+(m−1)r and is nonconstant when r=0. Using d for the common difference and numbering the first sequence term as a1​, its explicit and recursive descriptions are
ak​=a1​+(k−1)d,ak+1​=ak​+d.
(36)
The explicit formula reaches any position directly; the recurrence reaches the next position from the current one. The factor k−1 counts the steps after the first entry. For real a1​,d, a positive common difference makes the sequence increase, a negative one makes it decrease, and zero makes it constant.[ref]
For an original example, start at seven and add three each time:
7,10,13,16,19,22,25,28,…,ak​=7+3(k−1).
(37)
The eighth entry is 7+7×3=28: eight sequence terms require seven increments. This counting principle makes arithmetic progressions useful for regularly spaced positions, repeated equal additions, and iteration over evenly spaced integers. The values need not be integers; starting at 1/2 with common difference 1/4 gives 1/2,3/4,1,5/4,….
A geometric progression instead holds a ratio constant. In the displayed arithmetic progression, 10/7 and 13/10 differ even though 10−7=13−10=3. Multiplying each entry by two would give a different kind of repeated update from adding three. Distinguishing the two rules matters before predicting later entries or adding the sequence terms.
Equal differences also appear in Nicomachus's treatment of arithmetic proportion. He describes successions of at least three numbers whose neighboring differences agree, then explains how regularly omitting counting numbers changes the common gap. This connects the progression to the arithmetic mean: a middle entry is equally far from its two neighbors.[ref]

Colour each interval [2j,2j+1)∩N by the parity of j. Every infinite arithmetic progression of positive common difference d meets every sufficiently large such interval, since the interval has length greater than d. Both colours occur infinitely often. For the eight-entry example, the sum is 8(7+28)/2=140, and the arithmetic mean of all eight entries is 17.5. A decreasing example 11,9,7,5,3,1 gives 6(11+1)/2=36. Negative values cause no algebraic difficulty: 3,1,−1,−3,−5 has sum 5(3−5)/2=−5.
The triangular number Tn​=1+2+⋯+n is the special case a1​=d=1, giving n(n+1)/2. More generally, an equal increase in each successive allocation makes the total grow as a quadratic function of the number of allocations. The eight-entry example has

Its first four entries add to 46, its first eight to 140, and its first twelve to 282. The sequence terms lie on a straight line when plotted against their sequence indices, while the partial sums follow a quadratic function.
